subject: Medicine
summary: Sickle cell disease is an inherited hemoglobin disorder causing rigid, sickle‑shaped red cells that lead to vaso‑occlusion, hemolytic anemia, and organ damage. Diagnosis relies on hemoglobin electrophoresis and peripheral smear; management focuses on preventing crises and infection.

sections.p: Sickle cell disease comprises a group of autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathies, most commonly HbSS, where a β‑globin mutation (Glu6Val) produces HbS. Under low oxygen, HbS polymerizes, distorting red cells.
b: Diagnostic criteria: HbS ≥ 50% on electrophoresis or HPLC, plus clinical features.
Peripheral smear shows sickle‑shaped RBCs, target cells, and Howell‑Jolly bodies.

t.b: Confirms type and proportion of HbS vs HbF/HbA; >90% HbS in homozygous disease.
Identifies sickle cells and degree of hemolysis; guides urgency of care.
Detects disease before symptoms; enables early prophylaxis.

sections.p: Severity is gauged by frequency of vaso‑occlusive crises, organ involvement, and laboratory markers (e.g., hemoglobin, LDH). The Pediatric Sickle Cell Disease Severity Score (PSCDSS) and adult complications index are used.
b: Mild: ≤2 crises/year, no organ damage.
Moderate: 3‑5 crises/year or early organ changes (e.g., splenomegaly).
Severe: >5 crises/year, stroke, pulmonary hypertension, or renal failure.

sections.p: The primary cause is the β‑globin point mutation (HbS). Co‑existing factors that worsen sickling are common in low‑resource settings.
b: HbSS genotype (most common cause).
Co‑inherited α‑thalassemia can modify severity.
Infections (malaria, bacterial sepsis, HIV) increase sickling risk.
Dehydration, hypoxia, acidosis, and extreme temperatures trigger crises.

sections.p: Patients present with chronic hemolytic anemia and acute vaso‑occlusive events. In infants, dactylitis is typical; older children and adults develop pain crises, splenic sequestration, and organ dysfunction.
b: Painful swelling of hands/feet (dactylitis) in <2 y.
Recurrent bone pain crises, often in long bones.
Anemia‑related fatigue, jaundice, gallstones.
Functional asplenia → fever = emergency.

sections.p: Beyond confirming diagnosis, labs assess hemolysis, organ function, and infection risk.
b: CBC with reticulocyte count evaluates anemia severity.
LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin track hemolysis.
Renal and liver panels monitor end‑organ damage.

t.b: Quantifies anemia and reticulocytosis; low Hb with high retic suggests hemolysis.
Elevated levels confirm ongoing hemolysis.
Screens for elevated cerebral blood flow velocity; predicts stroke risk.
Detects acute chest syndrome; infiltrates require urgent care.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require rapid intervention.
b: Acute chest syndrome: fever, chest pain, hypoxia.
Stroke: focal neurologic deficit, seizures.
Splenic sequestration: sudden abdominal fullness, drop in Hb.
Severe infection (especially encapsulated bacteria).

sections.p: Treatment combines disease‑modifying therapy, crisis prevention, and supportive care.
b: Hydroxyurea increases HbF, reducing crises; first‑line disease‑modifying drug.
Penicillin prophylaxis (until age 5) prevents pneumococcal sepsis.
Vaccinations: pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, influenza.
Acute pain: IV opioids, hydration, oxygen if hypoxic.
Blood transfusion for severe anemia, stroke prevention, or ACS.

sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents complications and guides therapy adjustments.
b: Quarterly clinic visits with CBC, HbF level, and growth assessment.
Annual transcranial Doppler in children 2‑16 y.
Education on hydration, temperature avoidance, and early fever reporting.
Thalassemia major – also causes severe anemia but lacks sickle cells.
G6PD deficiency – hemolysis triggered by oxidative stress, not vaso‑occlusion.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia – positive Coombs test, no sickling.
Fetal hemoglobin may be high in early infancy, masking sickling on smear.
Normal peripheral smear in early disease if sample taken during a transfusion.
Low HbF after hydroxyurea non‑adherence can be misinterpreted as disease progression.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever >38 °C in any child with SCD (risk of sepsis).
Chest pain, shortness of breath, or new infiltrate on X‑ray (acute chest syndrome).
Sudden severe abdominal pain with rapid Hb drop (splenic sequestration).

faq.q: Why do patients with SCD become functionally asplenic?
faq.a: Repeated splenic infarction from sickling destroys splenic tissue, eliminating its ability to clear encapsulated bacteria.
It increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which inhibits HbS polymerization, reducing sickling and pain crises.

faq.q: When is a blood transfusion indicated?
faq.a: For severe anemia, acute chest syndrome, stroke prevention, or splenic sequestration with rapid Hb decline.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of vaso‑occlusive crises and how hydroxyurea modifies it.
List the acute complications of sickle cell disease that require immediate hospitalization.
Interpret a hemoglobin electrophoresis report showing 90% HbS, 5% HbF, and 5% HbA2.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam reveal the pattern of vaso‑occlusion, hemolysis and organ involvement while excluding mimics.
b: Age at first symptoms and any dactylitis before 2 years.
Frequency, location and triggers of painful crises in the past 12 months.
History of acute chest syndrome, stroke, priapism, leg ulcers or splenic sequestration.
Recent fever, cough, dyspnoea, jaundice, dark urine, or abdominal pain.
Vaccination status (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib) and prophylactic penicillin use.
Transfusion history, iron overload signs, and chelation therapy.
Comorbidities: HIV, TB, malaria, pregnancy, renal or hepatic disease, malnutrition, alcohol or herbal use.

t.b: Look for pallor, jaundice, scleral icterus, growth failure; positive indicates chronic anemia or hemolysis but cannot quantify severity.
Detect murmur of high‑output state or pulmonary hypertension; a loud P2 suggests pulmonary hypertension but cannot confirm without echo.
Palpate for splenomegaly (soft, tender tip) or hepatomegaly; presence indicates sequestration or chronic congestion, but size estimation is imprecise.

t.a: Peripheral smear (bedside smear if microscope available)
t.b: Identify sickled cells, target cells, Howell‑Jolly bodies; confirms sickling morphology but cannot replace quantitative electrophoresis.
Assess for crackles, decreased breath sounds; suggests acute chest syndrome but cannot differentiate infection from infarction.

t.a: Genital exam in males with priapism
t.b: Erection lasting >4 hours, rigid corpora cavernosa; indicates sickle cell priapism, but bedside exam cannot determine underlying ischemia.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Laboratory and imaging tests answer specific questions about hemoglobin composition, hemolysis, organ function and risk of complications.
b: Serum LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin – hemolysis panel; LDH >600 U/L, indirect bilirubin >2 mg/dL, low haptoglobin support hemolysis.
Renal panel (creatinine, eGFR, uric acid) – assesses renal impairment; eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² signals chronic kidney disease.
Liver panel and ultrasound – evaluates cholestasis, gallstones; gallstones in SCD are black pigment stones.
Chest X‑ray or CT – identifies acute chest syndrome; new infiltrate plus fever or hypoxia confirms.
Blood cultures and malaria smear – rule out infection in fever; positive culture mandates targeted antibiotics.

t.b: Question: Is sickle cell disease present? Result: HbS >85 % with absent HbA confirms HbSS; HbS 40‑60 % with HbA present suggests trait.
Question: Is iron overload present? Result: Ferritin consistently >1000 ng/mL or >20 transfusions warrants chelation; single isolated rise is insufficient.
Question: Is hemoglobinuria present? Positive dipstick with no RBCs suggests intravascular hemolysis; cannot differentiate from myoglobinuria.
Question: Is pulmonary hypertension present? Elevated tricuspid regurgitant velocity >2.5 m/s suggests PH; requires confirmatory right‑heart cath.
Use clinical surrogates: for TCD, refer for MRI/MRA if possible; for electrophoresis, use sickle cell solubility test plus family history.

sections.p: Classification integrates genotype, crisis frequency and end‑organ damage to guide therapy.
b: Genotype: HbSS or HbSβ0‑thalassemia = severe; HbSC or HbSβ+‑thalassemia = moderate.
Moderate disease: 3‑5 crises/year or early organ changes (splenomegaly, mild pulmonary hypertension).
Laboratory severity markers: reticulocyte count >10 %, LDH >800 U/L, ferritin >1000 ng/mL.
Imaging severity: TCD velocity >200 cm/s, echocardiographic TR velocity >2.5 m/s.

sections.p: Several disorders mimic sickle cell presentations; careful history, labs and imaging separate them.

t.b: Points: microcytic anemia, transfusion dependence, skeletal deformities. Separate by electrophoresis showing absent HbS and elevated HbF/HbA2.
Points: sudden drop in Hb, positive Coombs test, no sickled cells. Separate by negative sickle prep and positive direct antiglobulin test.
Points: episodic hemolysis after oxidative stress, bite cells, Heinz bodies. Separate by enzyme assay and absence of HbS on electrophoresis.
Points: fever, hemolysis, splenomegaly in endemic area. Separate by peripheral smear showing parasites, not sickled cells.
Points: joint pain, swelling, fever. Separate by joint aspiration showing purulent fluid, not bone infarction.

sections.p: A clear, tiered approach ensures rapid relief and prevents complications. Begin with immediate supportive care, then target the underlying pathophysiology, monitor response, and know when to intensify or transfer.
b: 1. Immediate assessment of airway, breathing, circulation; give IV access and fluids to maintain euvolemia.
3. Administer broad‑spectrum antibiotics if fever or infection suspected; cover pneumococcus and staphylococci.
6. Monitor vital signs, pain score, urine output, and laboratory indices every 4–6 hours.
7. Escalate to intensive care if hypoxia, hemodynamic instability, or refractory pain; refer to tertiary centre if exchange transfusion or advanced imaging unavailable.

t.b: Increases HbF, reduces sickling; monitor CBC, adjust dose if neutrophils <2.0×10⁹/L or platelets <80×10⁹/L.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognise common adverse effects and interactions to avoid treatment failure or harm.
b: Opioids: risk of respiratory depression; monitor SpO₂, provide naloxone if needed.
NSAIDs: avoid in renal impairment; use acetaminophen instead.

t.b: Hold hydroxyurea, give growth factors if severe; resume when counts recover.
Adjust NSAIDs or avoid; monitor creatinine and electrolytes.

sections.p: Certain presentations mandate urgent escalation to prevent mortality.
b: Acute chest syndrome: chest pain, fever, hypoxia; transfer to ICU, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, consider exchange transfusion.
Stroke: focal deficit, seizures; urgent neuroimaging, exchange transfusion, blood pressure control.
Severe sepsis: high fever, hypotension, organ dysfunction; start IV fluids, broad antibiotics, consider ICU.
Gastrointestinal bleeding: melena, hematemesis; stabilize, transfuse, endoscopy if available.

t.b: Urgent CT/MRI, exchange transfusion, maintain HbS <30%.

sections.p: Co‑existing conditions alter presentation, investigations, and therapy.
b: HIV: increases infection risk; ensure ART adherence, avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
TB: can mimic chest syndrome; screen with sputum X‑pert, treat per guidelines.
Malnutrition: reduces drug metabolism; adjust doses, provide nutrition support.
Pregnancy: increased blood volume, risk of preeclampsia; avoid teratogenic drugs, monitor fetal growth.
Diabetes: worsens infection risk; control glucose, monitor renal function.
Herbal remedies: some contain quinine or antimalarials; review for drug interactions.
Alcohol: hepatotoxicity, worsens anemia; counsel abstinence.
Renal failure: limits hydroxyurea and NSAID use; adjust transfusion thresholds.
Liver failure: monitor bilirubin, avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
Age extremes: infants need higher fluid rates; elderly need careful opioid titration.

t.b: Use ART, avoid nephrotoxic drugs, monitor CD4 and viral load.
Avoid teratogens, use hydroxyurea only after 3rd trimester if necessary, monitor fetal growth.

sections.p: Tailor management to unique physiological and resource constraints.
b: Elderly: higher risk of infection and renal impairment; use lower opioid doses, monitor renal function.
HIV patients: ensure ART, avoid drug interactions, monitor for opportunistic infections.
Low‑resource settings: prioritize oral hydroxyurea, use simple CBC and reticulocyte count, rely on clinical assessment for chest syndrome, use packed RBCs for transfusion.

t.b: Use age‑appropriate pain assessment, start hydroxyurea early, monitor growth and CBC.
Rely on clinical signs for chest syndrome, use simple labs, prioritize hydroxyurea over expensive transfusion.

facts: HbSS diagnosis: >85% HbS, 0% HbA on electrophoresis or HPLC.
Neutrophil count <2.0×10^9/L or platelets <80×10^9/L triggers hydroxyurea dose reduction or pause.
Acute chest syndrome: fever, chest pain, hypoxia, new infiltrate on chest X‑ray.
Stroke transfusion target: HbS <30% and Hb ≥10 g/dL.
Hydroxyurea increases HbF, reduces HbS polymerisation and leukocyte adhesion.
Functional asplenia: fever in SCD patient = emergency; treat with IV antibiotics and supportive care.

vivas.q: Define sickle cell disease and its most common genotype.
vivas.a: Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathy caused by a β‑globin point mutation; the most common genotype is HbSS.

vivas.q: What is the diagnostic criterion for HbSS on electrophoresis?
vivas.a: HbSS shows >85% HbS and 0% HbA; HbS ≥50% indicates sickle cell trait.

vivas.q: Explain the pathophysiology of a vaso‑occlusive crisis.
vivas.a: Deoxygenated HbS polymerises, causing RBC sickling, increased rigidity, microvascular occlusion, ischemia, and pain; inflammation and leukocyte adhesion amplify the process.

vivas.q: Why is hydroxyurea started early in children with HbSS?
vivas.a: It raises HbF, reduces sickling and crises; guidelines recommend starting from 6–9 months regardless of crisis frequency.

vivas.q: Interpret a hemoglobin electrophoresis showing 90% HbS, 5% HbF, 5% HbA2.
vivas.a: This pattern confirms HbSS; the small HbF is normal for adults; HbA2 is within normal limits.

vivas.q: A 28‑year‑old with priapism and SCD: first‑line urological treatment?
vivas.a: Immediate aspiration of corpora cavernosa and intracavernosal injection of a sympathomimetic (e.g., phenylephrine).

vivas.q: Which organism poses greatest danger for severe infection in adult SCD?
vivas.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common and dangerous pathogen; hence pneumococcal vaccination is critical.

vivas.q: What clinical finding characterises hand‑foot syndrome in young children?
vivas.a: Painful swelling of the hands and feet, often with erythema and warmth, due to vaso‑occlusion of small bones.

vivas.q: Which imaging modality identifies children at high risk for stroke?
vivas.a: Transcranial Doppler ultrasound; velocities >200 cm/s predict stroke risk.

vivas.q: Describe the management goals for SCD.
vivas.a: Prevent crises, reduce hemolysis, maintain organ function, prevent infections, and improve quality of life through hydroxyurea, transfusion, vaccination, and education.

vivas.q: Why is pethidine avoided in SCD pain management?
vivas.a: Its metabolite normeperidine accumulates, causing seizures; safer opioids are preferred.

vivas.q: What is the target HbS percentage after exchange transfusion in acute stroke?
vivas.a: Reduce HbS to <30% while maintaining Hb ≥10 g/dL.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a fever in a patient with functional asplenia?
vivas.a: It indicates a potential overwhelming infection; immediate IV antibiotics and supportive care are mandatory.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the best first‑line treatment for a vaso‑occlusive crisis?
mcqs.e: Morphine provides rapid analgesia for severe pain.

cases.v: A 5‑year‑old boy with HbSS presents with fever, pallor, and a painful swelling of the left foot. CBC shows Hb 7.5 g/dL, reticulocytes 8%, LDH 450 IU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

qs.a: Start IV fluids, analgesia with opioids, and monitor for infection.
If HbS >50% and signs of organ dysfunction or severe anemia.

cases.v: A 30‑year‑old woman with HbSS presents with sudden chest pain, dyspnoea, and a new infiltrate on chest X‑ray. She is afebrile. What is the next step in management?

qs.a: Give IV morphine, oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94%, and broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
If hypoxia persists or HbS >50% with organ compromise.

mistakes: Assuming HbS ≥50% alone diagnoses SCD; requires >85% HbS and 0% HbA.
Starting pain crises with only acetaminophen; opioids should be first line for severe pain.
Ignoring neutropenia or thrombocytopenia when adjusting hydroxyurea dose.
Overlooking functional asplenia; fever in SCD is an emergency.
Misinterpreting black pigment stones as cholesterol stones; they are pigmented due to haemolysis.
Failing to give both PCV13 and PPSV23; only PCV13 is insufficient.
Not recognising the need for exchange transfusion in acute stroke to reduce HbS below 30%.
Using pethidine for pain; it can cause seizures due to normeperidine accumulation.
